chapter.name: Patterns in Life: Diversity and Classification

questions.q: Which statement correctly describes an endemic species?
o: A species found naturally only in a particular region and nowhere else
A species found naturally in many different regions of the world
A species that has recently been declared extinct in the wild
A species that is allowed to live only inside a national park
questions.a: A species found naturally only in a particular region and nowhere else, such as the Nilgiri tahr, which is found only in India.

questions.q: The chapter names some global biodiversity hotspots that include parts of India. Which of these regions is NOT one of them?
questions.a: The Thar Desert. The hotspots the chapter names are the Western Ghats, Indo-Burma (including North East India), the Himalayas and Sundaland (including the Nicobar Islands).

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about India's biodiversity.
I. Each natural region of India, such as the northern mountains or the southern plateaus, has its own soil types and climatic conditions.
II. Neelakurinji is the Indian variety of the pitcher plant.
III. Sundaland, one of the global biodiversity hotspots, includes the Nicobar Islands.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: I and III only. Statement II is wrong: the Indian variety of the pitcher plant is Nepenthes khasiana; Neelakurinji is a different plant found only in India.

questions.q: True or False: 'New forms of life arose because small differences among individuals, which affected their chances of survival and reproduction, built up over many generations.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says small differences among individuals helped them adapt to changed conditions; these differences accumulated over many generations and gave rise to new forms of life, so today's diversity is the outcome of continuous change over a vast span of time.
s: Verdict: True
Reason: the differences helped survival and reproduction, accumulated over many generations and gave rise to new forms of life

questions.q: A Class 9 nature club lists what it saw on a trip: a glowing jellyfish, an eagle, a mushroom on a log and green algae in a pond. (a) What term does the chapter use for this immense variety of living organisms? (b) State one way, given in the chapter, in which humans depend on this variety.
questions.a: (a) Biodiversity. (b) Humans depend on it for food, shelter, medicines or livelihoods (any one).
s: (a) biodiversity
(b) any one of food, shelter, medicines, livelihoods

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The Western Ghats is a global biodiversity hotspot.
Reason (R): India has long coastlines along the Arabian Sea and the Bay of Bengal.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: the Western Ghats is a hotspot because it supports a large number of endemic species and has undergone significant habitat loss; having a coastline is not what makes a region a hotspot.

questions.q: The chapter says that forests rich in biodiversity create physical, biological and chemical barriers that protect against harm. For each example, say which kind of barrier it is and how it protects. (a) Mangrove forests during the 1999 super cyclone in Orissa. (b) Many kinds of forest animals in the Western Ghats and Kyasanur Forest Disease (monkey fever). (c) Diverse microorganisms in forest soils and plant roots.
questions.a: (a) Physical barrier: the large diversity of mangrove trees stood against the cyclone, and villages with more mangroves had less destruction. (b) Biological barrier: many of the forest animals are hosts in which the virus cannot replicate, so rich diversity lowers the risk of the disease. (c) Chemical barrier: the microorganisms absorb, transform or break down pollutants, which improves water quality and protects ecosystems.
s: (a) physical barrier: mangroves reduced cyclone damage to villages
(b) biological barrier: many hosts in which the virus cannot replicate lower the disease risk
(c) chemical barrier: microorganisms absorb or break down pollutants and improve water quality

questions.q: A village in the Western Ghats protects a 12-hectare sacred grove. A college survey finds 86 plant species in the grove, of which 18 grow naturally only in the Western Ghats. A neighbouring 12-hectare coffee estate has 23 plant species, of which 2 grow only in the Western Ghats. A road must be widened: one plan cuts 3 hectares out of the grove and costs Rs 40 lakh; the other goes around the grove and costs Rs 1.1 crore. (a) How many more plant species does the grove hold than the estate? (b) What percentage of the grove's plant species grow only in the Western Ghats? (c) How does the custom of sacred groves help keep such diversity, according to the chapter? (d) The Western Ghats is a biodiversity hotspot. Which plan should the panchayat choose? Justify using your answers and what makes a region a hotspot.
questions.a: (a) 86 - 23 = 63 more species. (b) 18 / 86 x 100 = about 20.9%. (c) Sacred groves are protected by custom, which preserves locally diverse habitats, in line with modern ecological principles. (d) The route around the grove is better justified: the grove holds far more species and many endemic ones, and a hotspot is a region that has many endemic species and has already suffered significant habitat loss, so cutting 3 hectares adds to that loss. The cost is Rs 1.1 crore - Rs 40 lakh = Rs 70 lakh more, which is the real price of the choice; an answer that picks the cheaper plan must show how the endemic species would be protected elsewhere.
s: (a) 63 more species
(b) about 20.9% endemic
(c) custom protects the grove and so preserves locally diverse habitat
(d) choose the route around, weighing Rs 70 lakh extra against further habitat loss in a hotspot with endemic species

questions.q: On a field trip to the Nilgiri hills, which are part of the Western Ghats, a class sees a Nilgiri tahr, learns that much of the region's forest has been cleared over the years, and finds dark, crumbly soil under a heap of fallen leaves. Answer each part in one or two lines. (a) The Nilgiri tahr is found naturally only in India. What kind of species is it? (b) Name one other such species of India given in the chapter. (c) Which two conditions make the Western Ghats a biodiversity hotspot? (d) Name the organisms that turn fallen leaves into manure. (e) Give one reason, from the chapter, why protecting hotspots matters.
questions.a: (a) An endemic species. (b) Lion-tailed macaque, Nepenthes khasiana (Indian pitcher plant) or Neelakurinji (any one). (c) It supports a large number of endemic species and has undergone significant habitat loss. (d) Fungi and bacteria, which decompose fallen leaves and convert waste into manure. (e) Hotspots support food webs and help ecosystems remain healthy (they are especially rich in the number and diversity of organisms).
s: (a) endemic species
(b) one of lion-tailed macaque, Nepenthes khasiana, Neelakurinji
(c) many endemic species and significant habitat loss
(d) fungi and bacteria
(e) they support food webs and keep ecosystems healthy

questions.q: Which pair of terms belongs to the classification criterion 'mode of nutrition'?
questions.a: Autotrophic or heterotrophic. Producer, consumer or decomposer is the ecological role; unicellular or multicellular is cell structure; asexual or sexual methods is reproduction.

questions.q: Meera sorts a neem tree, a deer and a fungus growing on a dead log into three groups labelled 'producer', 'consumer' and 'decomposer'. Which classification criterion from the chapter is she using?
questions.a: Ecological role: the chapter lists producer, consumer or decomposer as the ecological role of an organism.

questions.q:
Match each classification criterion in Column I with what it looks at in Column II.
Column I: 1. External features  2. Cell structure  3. Reproduction  4. Genetic similarity
Column II: (p) shape, size and body organisation  (q) presence or absence of a cell wall  (r) asexual and/or sexual methods  (s) similarities in inherited features, studied using DNA
questions.a: 1-p, 2-q, 3-r, 4-s: external features are shape, size and body organisation; cell structure includes the presence or absence of a cell wall; reproduction is asexual and/or sexual; genetic similarity is studied in detail using DNA.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): An owl and a bat can be put in the same group by one criterion and in different groups by another.
Reason (R): The group an organism falls into depends on the criterion chosen for grouping.
o: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A: grouped by when they are active, both are night animals, but grouped by body covering, the owl (feathers) and the bat fall apart, because the same organism fits different groups depending on the criterion.

questions.q: (a) According to the chapter, what do similar features in a group of organisms suggest about their origin? (b) Which classification criterion do scientists study in detail using DNA?
questions.a: (a) That the organisms have evolved from common ancestors. (b) Genetic similarity (similarities in inherited features).
s: (a) they evolved from common ancestors
(b) genetic similarity

questions.q: Name the classification criterion from the chapter's list that each observation uses. (a) 'The animal's body is supported by a skeleton of bones.' (b) 'Its cell has no cell wall.' (c) 'It produces offspring both asexually and sexually.'
questions.a: (a) Internal structures (skeletal patterns). (b) Cell structure (presence or absence of a cell wall). (c) Reproduction (asexual and/or sexual methods).
s: (a) internal structures
(b) cell structure
(c) reproduction

questions.q: Kavya says, 'If two organisms look alike from the outside, they must be closely related, so external features are all a scientist needs to classify them.' Check her claim using the chapter.
questions.a: Partly right. Similar features do suggest that organisms evolved from common ancestors. But external features are only the broad, easily visible ones; scientists then look at more detailed features such as internal structures, cell structure and genetic similarity (studied using DNA). The same organisms can also be grouped differently when the criterion changes, so looking alike from outside is not enough on its own.
s: Agrees that similar features suggest common ancestry
Scientists also use detailed criteria: internal structures, cell structure, genetic similarity
Verdict: partly right; external look alone is not enough

questions.q: A student proposes that all living organisms should first be divided by one criterion: 'Does it have xylem and phloem?' (a) Name three organisms from three different kingdoms that would all fall in the 'no xylem and phloem' group. (b) Why does this make it a poor first criterion for all of life? (c) Name the criterion that separates Monera from every other kingdom. (d) Give one reason why cellular organisation suits all organisms as a basis of classification. (e) Where in classification is the presence of xylem and phloem actually useful?
questions.a: (a) For example a bacterium (Monera), Amoeba (Protista) and a mushroom (Fungi); a moss and every animal would also join them. (b) Xylem and phloem occur only in some plants, so the criterion lumps together very different organisms, such as a bacterium and a tiger, and says nothing about most of life. (c) Cell type: Monera are prokaryotes, with no true membrane-bound nucleus, while all other kingdoms are eukaryotes. (d) Every organism is made of one or more cells, so cell type, cell structure and level of organisation can be checked for all of them; that is why they form the basis of the five kingdom classification. (e) Within Kingdom Plantae, to separate classes: pteridophytes such as ferns have xylem and phloem, while bryophytes lack vascular tissues.
s: (a) three organisms from three kingdoms that lack xylem and phloem
(b) only some plants have it, so unlike organisms are lumped together
(c) cell type: prokaryote with no true nucleus
(d) every organism has cells, so the criterion applies to all; basis of five kingdoms
(e) useful only within Plantae to separate classes

questions.q: Who proposed the five kingdom classification, and in which year?
questions.a: Robert H. Whittaker, 1969. Copeland gave the four kingdom system (1938), Haeckel the three kingdom system (1866) and Linnaeus the two kingdom system (1758).

questions.q: A scientist in the year 1900 uses Haeckel's three kingdom system. Where would she place a bacterium and an amoeba?
o: The bacterium in Monera and the amoeba in Protista
The bacterium in Plantae and the amoeba in Animalia
questions.a: Both in Protista: the third kingdom, Protista, was added for unicellular microscopic organisms. Monera was split off for bacteria only in the four kingdom system of 1938, after microscopes showed that bacteria lack a true nucleus.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about how classification changed over time.
I. Aristotle grouped animals using the cell structure he saw under a microscope.
II. The two kingdom system was introduced in the 18th century.
III. Fungi were given a kingdom of their own because they do not make their own food but absorb nutrients.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: II and III only. Statement I is wrong: Aristotle grouped animals by habitat (land, water, air) and by external appearance; his system relied on easily observable features, not on cells.

questions.q: True or False: 'Whittaker's five kingdom classification is final, so it will never need to change.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. Classification is an ongoing process: as new tools such as better microscopes and genetic (DNA) studies give new knowledge, classification systems are changed; the five kingdom system still could not fully explain the diversity of life.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: classification keeps changing as new tools and knowledge, such as DNA studies, appear

questions.q: (a) In the two kingdom system, which two features defined an organism of Plantae? (b) Which two features defined an organism of Animalia?
questions.a: (a) Plantae: organisms that do not move from one place to another and synthesise their own food. (b) Animalia: organisms that move from one place to another and depend on other organisms for food.
s: (a) Plantae: do not move, make their own food
(b) Animalia: move, depend on other organisms for food

questions.q: Each organism below was at some point given a kingdom of its own name. Name that kingdom and the classification system (with its year) that first gave it. (a) Paramecium (b) a bacterium (c) a mushroom
questions.a: (a) Protista, in the three kingdom system (Haeckel, 1866). (b) Monera, in the four kingdom system (Copeland, 1938). (c) Fungi, in the five kingdom system (Whittaker, 1969).
s: (a) Protista, three kingdom system, 1866
(b) Monera, four kingdom system, 1938
(c) Fungi, five kingdom system, 1969

questions.q: Euglena is a single-celled organism that moves about in water and also makes its own food in sunlight. Show that it cannot be placed satisfactorily in either kingdom of the two kingdom system.
questions.a: Plantae are organisms that do not move and make their own food: Euglena makes its own food but moves, so it does not fit. Animalia are organisms that move and depend on others for food: Euglena moves but makes its own food, so it does not fit. Besides, plants and animals are multicellular while Euglena is unicellular. So it fits neither kingdom, which is the kind of problem that led to a third kingdom, Protista.
s: Does not fit Plantae: it moves
Does not fit Animalia: it makes its own food
Also unicellular while plants and animals are multicellular; hence Protista was needed

questions.q: A school museum puts up a wall panel on classification. It reads: 'In the 4th century BCE, Aristotle grouped animals by habitat: land, water and air. In 1758 Linnaeus divided life into Plantae and Animalia. In 1866 Haeckel added a third kingdom. In 1938 Copeland separated bacteria into a new kingdom. In 1969 Whittaker separated one more group, giving five kingdoms.' (a) Name the four kingdoms of Copeland's system. (b) How many years passed between Haeckel's and Copeland's systems? (c) What did improved microscopes show that led Copeland to separate bacteria? (d) Which group did Whittaker separate, and why?
questions.a: (a) Plantae, Animalia, Protista and Monera. (b) 1938 - 1866 = 72 years. (c) An amoeba has a true, membrane-bound nucleus but bacteria do not, so the two could not stay in one kingdom. (d) Fungi: they do not move, like plants, but are heterotrophic and obtain nutrients by absorption, so they were placed in a kingdom of their own.
s: (a) Plantae, Animalia, Protista, Monera
(b) 72 years
(c) bacteria lack a true nucleus while amoeba has one
(d) Fungi, heterotrophic and absorb nutrients

questions.q: A student suggests going back to a single kingdom for all unicellular organisms: bacteria, Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena and yeast. In this list Euglena makes its own food in sunlight, while Amoeba and Paramecium depend on other organisms for food. Explain the problems this would create: (a) the difference in cell type it would hide; (b) the difference in mode of nutrition it would hide; (c) why yeast in particular does not belong with the others; (d) which step in the history of classification it would undo.
questions.a: (a) Bacteria are prokaryotes with no true nucleus, while the others are eukaryotes with a membrane-bound nucleus. (b) Euglena is autotrophic while Amoeba and Paramecium are heterotrophic, so feeding methods would be mixed in one group. (c) Yeast, though unicellular, has a cell wall made of chitin, which is why it is placed in Kingdom Fungi. (d) It would undo the four kingdom system of 1938, in which bacteria were separated as Monera because they lack a true nucleus (and the later separation of Fungi).
s: (a) prokaryote bacteria mixed with eukaryotes
(b) autotrophs mixed with heterotrophs
(c) yeast has a chitin cell wall, so it is a fungus
(d) undoes the separation of Monera in 1938

questions.q: Which kingdom is made up of unicellular prokaryotes such as bacteria, archaea and cyanobacteria?
questions.a: Monera: its members are single-celled and have no true (membrane-bound) nucleus.

questions.q: The fungus Aspergillus and the bacterium Rhizobium are both useful to people. Which difference places them in DIFFERENT kingdoms?
o: Aspergillus cells have a true nucleus, while Rhizobium cells do not
Aspergillus is useful to people, while Rhizobium is harmful
Aspergillus makes its own food, while Rhizobium cannot
Aspergillus lives in soil, while Rhizobium lives only in water
questions.a: Aspergillus cells have a true nucleus, while Rhizobium cells do not: a fungus is a eukaryote, while a bacterium is a prokaryote of Kingdom Monera. Usefulness and habitat do not decide the kingdom, and fungi do not make their own food.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Without fungi, the decay of dead plants and animals would be greatly reduced and soil fertility would suffer.
Reason (R): Fungi make their own food by photosynthesis and add it to the soil.
o: A is true, but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: A is true, but R is false: fungi do not make their own food; they are heterotrophs that absorb nutrients from dead and decaying matter and, as decomposers, break it down into simpler substances that become minerals in the soil.

questions.q:
Match Column I with Column II.
Column I: 1. Lactobacillus  2. Penicillium  3. Cyanobacteria  4. Ram Bux Singh
Column II: (p) a useful bacterium  (q) a fungus used to make enzymes and antibiotics  (r) among the first organisms to produce oxygen by photosynthesis  (s) known as the 'Father of Modern Biogas'
questions.a: 1-p, 2-q, 3-r, 4-s: Lactobacillus is a useful bacterium, Penicillium is used to make enzymes and antibiotics, cyanobacteria were among the first oxygen producers, and Ram Bux Singh is the Father of Modern Biogas.

questions.q: In Activity 12.5, a hay infusion is kept for a week and a drop of it is seen under a microscope. (a) Name two protists you may be able to identify in the drop. (b) State two precautions the chapter gives for handling the hay infusion.
questions.a: (a) Any two of Amoeba, Paramecium and Euglena. (b) Wear a lab coat, mask and hand gloves; discard the hay infusion after autoclaving.
s: (a) two of Amoeba, Paramecium, Euglena
(b) wear lab coat, mask and gloves; discard after autoclaving

questions.q: A chemical leak kills most of the protists in a village pond, but the small animals in it are not harmed directly. (a) State two roles that protists play in aquatic food chains, according to the chapter. (b) Predict one effect of the leak on the small animals of the pond, giving a reason.
questions.a: (a) Some protists produce oxygen, while others serve as food for small animals (some also act as decomposers and help in nutrient cycling). (b) The small animals that feed on protists would have less food, so their numbers would fall (they may also get less oxygen).
s: (a) protists produce oxygen and serve as food for small animals
(b) small animals lose a food source, so their numbers fall

questions.q: An organism found on a damp, rotting fruit is multicellular, has a cell wall, has no chlorophyll, grows best in warm and moist weather and spreads by spores. Rahul says, 'It has a cell wall and does not move, so it is a plant.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. Plants are autotrophs with a cell wall made of cellulose that make their own food by photosynthesis; this organism has no chlorophyll, so it cannot make its own food and must absorb nutrients from the rotting fruit. Its spores, its growth in warm, moist conditions and its feeding on dead matter are features of Kingdom Fungi, whose cell walls are made of chitin. A cell wall and not moving are shared by plants and fungi, so they cannot settle the kingdom.
s: No chlorophyll, so it cannot make its own food as plants do
Spores, warm moist growth and feeding on dead matter point to Fungi (chitin wall)
Verdict: Rahul is wrong; cell wall and not moving do not decide the kingdom

questions.q: A school collects about 1,800 kg of fallen leaves from its campus every year and has been burning them. The eco-club proposes a shaded compost pit instead. Assume 30% of the leaf mass becomes manure, and that the school now buys manure for its garden at Rs 8 per kg. (a) Name the two groups of organisms that will turn the leaves into manure, and their ecological role. (b) How much manure will the pit give in a year? (c) How much money can the school save in a year? (d) Why should the pit be kept moist? (e) Should the school switch to composting? Give a justified decision.
questions.a: (a) Fungi and bacteria, acting as decomposers that break down complex organic matter into simpler substances and minerals. (b) 30% of 1,800 kg = 540 kg of manure. (c) 540 x Rs 8 = Rs 4,320 a year. (d) Fungi grow best in warm and moist conditions, so moisture speeds up decay. (e) Yes: composting returns the minerals in the leaves to the soil and makes it fertile, saves Rs 4,320 a year, and avoids the smoke of burning; the cost is only the space and care of a pit, which the saving justifies.
s: (a) fungi and bacteria as decomposers
(b) 540 kg of manure
(c) Rs 4,320 saved
(d) fungi grow best in warm, moist conditions
(e) decision to compost, justified by soil fertility and the saving

questions.q: At a fossil site in Rajasthan, a guide shows layered rock mounds called stromatolites. The board says they were built by ancient cyanobacteria, which were among the first organisms to release oxygen by photosynthesis, and that oxygen began to collect in the atmosphere about 2.5 billion years ago. Cyanobacteria still live in water bodies today. (a) In which kingdom are cyanobacteria placed, and which cell feature decides this? (b) Name the other two groups of organisms that share this kingdom. (c) Why was the build-up of oxygen important for later life? (d) A visitor says, 'Cyanobacteria photosynthesise, so they should be in Kingdom Plantae.' Judge the claim using the criteria of the five kingdom classification.
questions.a: (a) Monera, because they are prokaryotes: their cells have no true, membrane-bound nucleus. (b) Bacteria and archaea. (c) The oxygen that accumulated in the atmosphere made the Earth suitable for other forms of life. (d) The claim is wrong. Mode of nutrition is only one criterion; the five kingdom system also uses cell type and level of organisation. Plants are multicellular eukaryotes with a cellulose cell wall, while cyanobacteria are unicellular prokaryotes, so they belong to Monera even though they are autotrophs.
s: (a) Monera; no true nucleus (prokaryote)
(b) bacteria and archaea
(c) oxygen made the Earth suitable for other life
(d) wrong: cell type and organisation place them in Monera though they are autotrophs

questions.q: Which plant class is called the 'amphibians' of the plant kingdom?
questions.a: Bryophyta: bryophytes such as mosses live on land but require water for reproduction, so they are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.

questions.q: A pond alga such as Spirogyra has neither roots nor xylem and phloem, yet each of its cells gets the water, nutrients and gases it needs. Which statement explains this and its effect on where the alga can live?
o: Its simple thallus exchanges these directly with the surrounding water, so it cannot live on land
Its rhizoids absorb these from the pond bed, so it can also live on damp land
Its needle-like leaves reduce water loss, so it can also live on dry land
Its cells pass water along a vascular tissue, so it can grow tall on land
questions.a: Its simple thallus exchanges water, nutrients and gases directly with the surrounding water, so it is well adapted to water but cannot live on land. Rhizoids belong to bryophytes, needle-like leaves to gymnosperms and vascular tissue to pteridophytes and higher plants.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Gymnosperms such as pines are well adapted to cold and dry regions.
Reason (R): The seeds of gymnosperms are not enclosed in fruits.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
questions.a: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A: gymnosperms suit cold and dry regions because their needle-like or scale-like leaves reduce water loss and they do not need water for fertilisation; seeds lying exposed on cones is a true fact but does not explain this.

questions.q:
Consider the following statements about Kingdom Plantae.
I. Thallophytes are mostly found on dry land.
II. Pteridophytes such as ferns produce seeds.
III. Angiosperms have the most complex body organisation among plants.
Which of the statements is/are correct?
questions.a: III only. Statement I is wrong because thallophytes are mostly found in water or moist places; statement II is wrong because pteridophytes do not produce seeds.

questions.q: True or False: 'Since bryophytes grow on land, they no longer depend on water for reproduction.' Give the verdict and a reason.
questions.a: False. Bryophytes require water for reproduction because their male reproductive cells must swim to reach the female cells; this is why they grow in moist, shady places and are called the amphibians of the plant kingdom.
s: Verdict: False
Reason: male reproductive cells must swim to the female cells, so water is needed

questions.q: A gardener in a hill town wants a tree that (i) survives cold, dry winters and (ii) has its seeds carried to new places by birds that eat its fruit. (a) Which plant class meets condition (i) but not condition (ii)? Give the reason. (b) Which plant class can meet condition (ii), and which feature of it does so?
questions.a: (a) Gymnosperms such as pine: their needle-like leaves reduce water loss and they need no water for fertilisation, but their seeds are not enclosed in fruits, so birds have no fruit to carry them. (b) Angiosperms: they produce fruits that enclose the seeds, and fruits help spread seeds to new places through animals such as birds.
s: (a) gymnosperm: suits cold, dry places but its seeds are not in fruits
(b) angiosperm: fruits enclose seeds and are spread by birds

questions.q: Plant class names carry a meaning. Explain how each name fits the plants in the class. (a) Gymnosperm ('naked seed') (b) Angiosperm ('vessel seed') (c) Thallophyta ('undifferentiated body plant')
questions.a: (a) Gymnosperm seeds are not enclosed in fruits; they lie exposed on cones, so they are 'naked'. (b) Angiosperm seeds are enclosed within fruits, which act as the 'vessel' holding the seeds. (c) A thallophyte such as Spirogyra has a simple thallus body that is not divided into root, stem and leaves.
s: (a) gymnosperm seeds are exposed on cones, not in fruits
(b) angiosperm seeds are enclosed in fruits (the vessel)
(c) thallophyte body is a simple thallus, not divided into parts

questions.q: On a nature walk, a class lists four plants. Place each in its class of Kingdom Plantae and give one feature that tells you so. (a) Marchantia growing as a green mat on a damp wall (b) a fern in a shaded, wet ravine (c) a pine bearing cones on a cold hillside (d) a gulmohar tree with bright flowers.
questions.a: (a) Bryophyta: it has root-like rhizoids and grows as a green mat in moist, shady places. (b) Pteridophyta: it has true roots, stems and leaves with xylem and phloem, but no seeds. (c) Gymnosperm: needle-like leaves and seeds exposed on cones. (d) Angiosperm: it produces flowers and fruits, with seeds enclosed in fruits.
s: (a) Bryophyta with a correct feature
(b) Pteridophyta with a correct feature
(c) Gymnosperm with a correct feature
(d) Angiosperm with a correct feature

questions.q: After a forest fire burnt a rocky hill slope bare, ecologists recorded which plants came back. In year 1, green mats of moss appeared only on damp, shaded rocks. In year 2, ferns grew in the wet hollows but not on the dry upper slope. By year 4, flowering shrubs had spread over the whole slope, mostly where birds perch. (a) Why did the moss grow only on damp, shaded rocks? (b) Ferns have true roots, stems, leaves and transport tissue, yet they stayed in the wet hollows. Why? (c) How did flowering shrubs spread across the slope, including the dry parts? (d) Which of these groups is best able to cover the dry upper slope, and why? Use two features.
questions.a: (a) Bryophytes depend strongly on moisture and need water for reproduction, as their male reproductive cells must swim. (b) Pteridophytes still need aquatic conditions for reproduction and produce no seeds, so they could only reproduce where it was wet. (c) Their seeds are enclosed in fruits, which birds and other animals carry to new places; this is why they appeared where birds perch. (d) The flowering shrubs (angiosperms): their reproduction depends on flowers, pollination and seeds rather than on standing water, seeds protect the embryo with stored food, and their fruits spread seeds widely, so they can occupy a wide range of environments.
s: (a) moss needs moisture and water for reproduction
(b) ferns need water for reproduction and have no seeds
(c) fruits carried by birds spread the seeds
(d) angiosperms, with two features such as seeds and fruit dispersal

questions.q: Sponges are multicellular animals whose bodies have many pores but no tissues or organs. To which phylum do they belong?
questions.a: Porifera, the pore-bearers: sponges are multicellular but lack organisation of tissues and organs.

questions.q: Which of these animals has a body with two openings, a mouth and an anus?
questions.a: A roundworm (Nematoda): its body has two openings, a mouth and an anus. Hydra and flatworms have a single opening for food intake and waste removal, and a sponge takes in water through many pores.

questions.q: Four features appear one after another as you move from simpler to more complex invertebrates: true tissues, then bilateral symmetry, then two body openings, then a segmented body. Which list gives, in the same order, the phylum in which the chapter first describes each feature?
questions.a: Cnidaria, Platyhelminthes, Nematoda, Annelida: tissue-level organisation first appears in cnidarians, bilateral symmetry in flatworms, two openings (mouth and anus) in roundworms, and a segmented body in annelids such as the earthworm.

questions.q: (a) Name the five groups into which vertebrates are classified. (b) State the three bases on which this grouping is made.
questions.a: (a) Fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds and mammals. (b) The broad patterns of their habitat use, body covering and reproduction.
s: (a) fish, amphibians, reptiles, birds, mammals
(b) habitat use, body covering, reproduction

questions.q: A Hydra in a pond catches small animals with its tentacles. (a) What two jobs does the single opening of its body have to do? (b) Suggest one limitation this gives Hydra compared with a roundworm.
questions.a: (a) The single opening is used both for taking in food and for removing waste. (b) A roundworm has two openings, so food enters at the mouth and waste leaves at the anus; Hydra must use one opening for both, so food intake and waste removal cannot go on separately at the same time.
s: (a) both food intake and waste removal
(b) a valid limitation compared with the roundworm's separate mouth and anus

questions.q: Tanvi says, 'A snail and a crab both have a hard outer covering, so they must belong to the same phylum.' Check her claim.
questions.a: No. A crab is an arthropod: it has a segmented body with segments specialised for different functions and jointed appendages, and its hard external skeleton supports powerful muscles. A snail is a mollusc: it has a soft body with a distinct head, a muscular foot and a hump, protected by a shell. Both have a hard outer covering, but their body plans differ, so one shared feature does not put them in the same phylum.
s: Crab: Arthropoda, segmented body with jointed appendages and exoskeleton
Snail: Mollusca, soft body with head, muscular foot and hump, protected by a shell
Verdict: Tanvi is wrong; one shared feature does not decide the phylum

questions.q: A museum curator is arranging six specimens along a trail called 'The story of the notochord': a sponge, an earthworm, a crab, a starfish, Amphioxus and a frog. (a) Which of the six have no notochord at any stage? (b) Where should Amphioxus go, and why? (c) Which specimen has a backbone, and what two jobs does the backbone do? (d) The curator wants to put the starfish next to the frog because both have an internal skeleton. Evaluate this choice.
questions.a: (a) The sponge, earthworm, crab and starfish: they are invertebrates (non-chordata). (b) Amphioxus is a protochordate: it has a notochord at least once in its life but no backbone, so it goes between the invertebrates and the vertebrates. (c) The frog, a vertebrate: its vertebral column supports the body and protects vital organs such as the brain and spinal cord. (d) The choice is misleading: the starfish's internal skeleton is made of calcium carbonate, but it has no notochord and is an echinoderm, an invertebrate. On a notochord trail it belongs with the invertebrates, though its internal skeleton can be noted as a step towards internal skeletal support.
s: (a) sponge, earthworm, crab, starfish
(b) Amphioxus is a protochordate with a notochord but no backbone
(c) frog; backbone supports the body and protects brain and spinal cord
(d) starfish has no notochord, so it goes with invertebrates despite its internal skeleton

questions.q: The chapter says new structural features in invertebrates improved feeding, movement and protection. For each feature below, name the phylum in which the chapter describes it and give one advantage it brings. (a) many pores in the body (b) tentacles (c) bilateral symmetry (d) a body divided into segments (e) a hard external skeleton
questions.a: (a) Porifera: water flowing through the pores brings food particles and oxygen to the cells and carries waste away. (b) Cnidaria: tentacles capture prey, so the animal does not depend on water currents to bring food. (c) Platyhelminthes: distinct head-tail and front-back regions allow better coordination of movement in one direction. (d) Annelida: segmentation gives greater flexibility and more precise control of movement. (e) Arthropoda: the exoskeleton gives protection, reduces water loss and supports powerful muscles, so arthropods survive in dry, exposed places.
s: (a) Porifera with the advantage of pores
(b) Cnidaria with the advantage of tentacles
(c) Platyhelminthes with the advantage of bilateral symmetry
(d) Annelida with the advantage of segmentation
(e) Arthropoda with the advantage of the exoskeleton

questions.q: Which list gives the levels of classification in the correct order, from the broadest group to the most specific?
o: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Class, Phylum, Order, Genus, Family, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Order, Class, Family, Genus, Species
Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Family, Order, Genus, Species
questions.a: Kingdom, Phylum, Class, Order, Family, Genus, Species: classification moves from very broad groups to smaller and more specific ones.

questions.q: The tiger (Panthera tigris) belongs to Family Felidae. The lion is Panthera leo. Which statement about the lion must be true?
o: It also belongs to Family Felidae
It belongs to the same species as the tiger
It must belong to a different family from the tiger
It may belong to a different class from the tiger
questions.a: It also belongs to Family Felidae: the lion shares the genus Panthera with the tiger, and every lower group is a part of the group above it, so the same genus means the same family, order, class, phylum and kingdom. The species names tigris and leo differ, so they are different species.

questions.q: (a) What are fossils, and where are they found? (b) In general, how do the organisms in older rock layers differ from those in newer layers?
questions.a: (a) Fossils are preserved remains of plants and animals, found in layers of rocks, sand and mud. (b) Older layers generally contain simpler organisms, while newer layers show more complex forms.
s: (a) preserved remains of plants and animals in layers of rock, sand and mud
(b) older layers simpler organisms, newer layers more complex

questions.q: (a) Name any two human activities that the chapter says are reducing biodiversity. (b) What may happen to other species when one species disappears?
questions.a: (a) Any two of pollution, deforestation, the overuse of resources and climate change. (b) Other species that depend on it may also decline in number and eventually disappear.
s: (a) any two of pollution, deforestation, overuse of resources, climate change
(b) species that depend on it may decline and disappear

questions.q: The scientific name of the Purple Frog of Kerala is Nasikabatrachus sahyadrensis. (a) Which word is the genus name, and how do you know? (b) After what is its species name given? (c) Why was its discovery in 2003 important?
questions.a: (a) Nasikabatrachus: the genus is the first word and begins with a capital letter. (b) The species name sahyadrensis is after the Sahyadri Hills, the place of its discovery. (c) It belongs to an ancient family of frogs known from fossils, so its discovery helped scientists understand ancient amphibian groups and highlighted the need for biodiversity conservation in the Western Ghats.
s: (a) Nasikabatrachus, first word with a capital letter
(b) named after the Sahyadri Hills
(c) helped understand ancient amphibians; showed need to conserve the Western Ghats

questions.q: In one rock section, Arjun finds that a newer layer holds a fossil that looks simpler than a fossil in the older layer below it. He says, 'This proves that fossils tell us nothing about how life has changed over time.' Check his claim.
questions.a: No. The chapter says that older layers GENERALLY contain simpler organisms and newer layers more complex forms; it is an overall pattern, so a single exception in one section does not overturn it. Fossils from many layers and places still act as natural records of how life has changed over millions of years. One odd pair can raise a question for further study, but it cannot show that fossils tell us nothing.
s: The pattern is a general one ('generally'), not a rule for every pair
Fossils from many layers are natural records of change over millions of years
Verdict: Arjun is wrong; one exception does not disprove the record

questions.q: A student hand-writes these scientific names in her notebook: (i) Panthera Leo, underlined (ii) mangifera indica, underlined (iii) Pisum sativum, underlined (iv) tigris Panthera, underlined. For each, say whether it is written correctly. If it is wrong, name the rule that is broken and write it correctly.
questions.a: (i) Wrong: the species name must be in small letters; correct form Panthera leo (underlined). (ii) Wrong: the genus name must begin with a capital letter; correct form Mangifera indica (underlined). (iii) Correct: genus first with a capital letter, species in small letters, underlined because it is handwritten. (iv) Wrong: the genus must come first, followed by the species; correct form Panthera tigris (underlined).
s: (i) wrong: species in lower case, Panthera leo
(ii) wrong: genus capitalised, Mangifera indica
(iii) correct as written
(iv) wrong: genus comes first, Panthera tigris

questions.q: In a mango-growing block of Andhra Pradesh, farmers sprayed pesticides heavily for six years and cut down the hedgerow trees between orchards. Over this time the number of wild bee hives counted in the orchards fell from 250 to 60, and the average number of mangoes set per tree fell from 400 to 260. Two plans are offered: Plan A is hand-pollination by hired workers at Rs 18,000 per hectare every season; Plan B is to cut spraying and replant hedgerows at a one-time cost of Rs 45,000 per hectare, with bees expected to return over about three seasons. (a) Find the percentage fall in bee hives and in mangoes per tree. (b) Using the chapter, explain why the mango crop fell along with the bees. (c) Which two human activities named in the chapter are at work here? (d) Over five seasons, which plan should the farmers choose? Justify, giving one drawback of your choice.
questions.a: (a) Hives: (250 - 60) / 250 x 100 = 76% fall. Mangoes: (400 - 260) / 400 x 100 = 35% fall. (b) Animals such as bees pollinate flowers; when one species declines, others that depend on it also decline, so fewer flowers were pollinated and fewer mangoes set. (c) Pollution (pesticides) and deforestation (cutting the hedgerow trees). (d) Plan B: over five seasons Plan A costs 5 x Rs 18,000 = Rs 90,000 per hectare against Rs 45,000 for Plan B, and Plan B restores the biodiversity that pollinates the crop. Its drawback is that bees take about three seasons to return, so yields stay low for a while unless some hand-pollination is used in the gap.
s: (a) 76% fall in hives and 35% fall in mangoes
(b) bees pollinate flowers; decline of one species affects those that depend on it
(c) pollution and deforestation
(d) Plan B, Rs 45,000 against Rs 90,000 over five seasons, with the slow-return drawback
